Elon Musk: The World's First Trillionaire.
Elon Musk is the world's first trillionaire.
Here's a look at how he got there.
Calculating that worth for someone like Elon Musk isn't easy.
A lot of his wealth is tied up in private companies, and valuing those can be a little tricky.
But his wealth primarily comes from three different buckets.
The largest part of that is his stake in SpaceX, which went public on Friday.
He owns about forty percent of it, so his stake is valued at about six hundred ninety billion dollars.
Now, pair that with a second bucket: his stake in the electric automaker Tesla.
That's valued at about two hundred seventy-one billion dollars at recent stock prices.
Musk also has a third, smaller bucket of miscellaneous assets.
Estimates from wealth intelligence firm Altrata put the value of his ownership in Neuralink, a brain-implant company,
at about five billion dollars — and at about the same valuation, the Boring Company.
He also has about one hundred four billion dollars of other assets: investments, a jet, property, that kind of thing.
Putting all those stakes together pushed him just over the one trillion dollars mark.
Elon Musk's wealth has grown dramatically just in the past year.
Late last summer, we estimated that he was worth just a little more than four hundred billion dollars.
A few weeks ago, we checked back: eight hundred eleven billion dollars.
And of course, now, he's crossed the trillion-dollar threshold.
Most of that huge increase since last summer is really about SpaceX.
Investors are very bullish about it, and that even managed to counteract some declines in Tesla's share price.
Musk's wealth is not money in the bank.
You can't just go out and spend it.
Almost all of it is tied up in these companies.
And of course, he's not only the biggest shareholder in these companies, he's also their leader.
If he starts selling, that could drive the share price down.
He can borrow against his holdings to some degree,
but ultimately his fortunes are tied up with the fortunes of these companies.
It's notable that this is happening at a time when a lot of Americans are struggling with the price of gas at the pump,
or other everyday costs like groceries and housing.
Wrapping your head around a trillion dollars is really hard.
It's one thousand billion dollars, but that doesn't really help much.
You could buy two point four million houses in the US with that kind of money.
You could buy every NFL and NBA team and have five hundred billion dollars left over.
It's about three percent of all the goods and services that the US produces in a year.
My colleagues and I have estimated that over the course of his career,
Elon Musk has built up wealth at an average of about one thousand dollars a second.
In the time that you've watched this video, that would work out to about this much.

How Elon Musk Became the First Trillionaire.
Elon Musk has become the world's first trillionaire.
So how did he reach this point?
Working out exactly how much someone like Musk is worth is not simple.
Much of his wealth is locked inside private companies, and putting a value on those can be tricky.
Still, his fortune comes mainly from three areas.
The biggest area is his share of SpaceX, the rocket company, which went public on Friday.
He owns roughly forty percent of it, and that share alone is worth about six hundred ninety billion dollars.
The second area is his share of Tesla, the electric car maker,
which is worth around two hundred seventy-one billion dollars at recent prices.
The third area is smaller and more mixed.
According to the research firm Altrata, his ownership of Neuralink, a brain-implant company, is worth about five billion dollars,
and his stake in the Boring Company is worth a similar amount.
On top of that, he owns about one hundred four billion dollars in other things — investments, a private jet,
property, and so on.
Added together, all of this pushes him just past the one trillion dollars line.
Musk's wealth has grown very quickly over the past year.
Late last summer, his fortune was estimated at a little over four hundred billion dollars.
A few weeks ago, it had reached eight hundred eleven billion dollars.
Now it has passed one trillion.
Most of this rapid growth comes from SpaceX, because investors are very confident about its future —
confident enough to cancel out the drop in Tesla's share price.
It is important to understand that this money is not sitting in a bank.
Musk cannot simply spend it, because almost all of it is tied to his companies.
He is not only the largest shareholder in these companies; he also runs them.
If he started selling his shares, the price could fall.
He can borrow money against what he owns, but in the end, his fortune rises and falls with these companies.
What makes this striking is the timing.
Many Americans are struggling with everyday costs such as gas, groceries, and housing.
A trillion dollars is very hard to imagine.
With that much money, you could buy two point four million American homes, or every NFL and NBA team —
and still have five hundred billion dollars left.
It equals about three percent of everything the United States produces in a year.
In fact, over his whole career,
Musk has built his wealth at an average of around one thousand dollars every second.

forbes-original.text:
What one trillion dollars Looks Like.
Elon Musk has become the world's first trillionaire, catapulted by the historic market debut of his rocket company, SpaceX.
The tech mogul has officially amassed thirteen-figure wealth.
SpaceX debuted on public markets Friday at one hundred fifty dollars a share,
locking in an unprecedented one point nine seven trillion dollars market valuation.
Ahead of the first trade, Forbes put Musk's net worth at nine hundred eighty-two billion dollars.
Much of his fortune comes from his electric car company, Tesla.
He also cofounded the company that later became PayPal.
One trillion dollars is one thousand times greater than one billion, and a million times greater than one million —
a one followed by twelve zeros, four commas.
Still, the number is hard to comprehend, so let's put it in perspective.
If you made one hundred thousand dollars a year and saved every penny,
it would take you ten million years to match that wealth.
That means you would have had to start working when early human ancestors were first walking the Earth.
If Musk decided to buy every single American adult a four dollars iced coffee every single day,
he could keep the entire country caffeinated for almost three years straight.
His wealth would sit just shy of the gross domestic product of Poland,
while completely eclipsing the entire annual economic output of Taiwan.
Only about twenty-one countries have a GDP higher than a trillion dollars today.
And if you divided up a trillion dollars equally among all eight point two billion people on Earth,
every single person on the planet would instantly get nearly one hundred twenty-two dollars.
So what does he plan to do with all that cash?
Musk says he doesn't plan to spend his trillion-dollar fortune solely on himself.
Instead, he'll use it to fund a permanent settlement on Mars —
and he's counting on SpaceX to get us there.

reuters-original.text:
What a one point one trillion dollars Fortune Really Means.
Elon Musk has become the world's first "on-paper" trillionaire.
But what does his reported wealth of over one point one trillion dollars actually mean?
For one thing, it is roughly equal to the GDP of Switzerland, the 20th-largest economy in the world.
If you were given a dollar every second,
it would take thirty-four thousand nine hundred years to reach one point one trillion dollars.
Going that far back in time would take you to the heyday of the woolly mammoth.
Laid end to end in dollar bills,
one point one trillion dollars would wrap around the sun one hundred thirty-nine times.
But Musk's arrival as the first member of the trillionaire club, thanks to his SpaceX IPO,
is also a powerful symbol of the gap between rich and poor.
In January, the global poverty charity Oxfam said billionaire wealth grew last year to its highest level on record —
eighteen point three trillion dollars —
even as one in four people struggle to eat regularly and half the world's population lives in poverty.
In a clash with Musk in 2021,
the World Food Programme produced a detailed plan showing how it would spend six point six billion dollars to save
forty-two million people who were on the brink of starvation.
With one point one trillion dollars, you could fund that plan for one hundred sixty-seven years.

reuters-b12.text:
One Fortune, and the Gap It Reveals.
Elon Musk has become the world's first trillionaire — at least "on paper.
" His reported wealth is now more than one point one trillion dollars,
but what does such a number actually mean?
To start with, it is roughly equal to the GDP of Switzerland, the 20th-largest economy in the world.
In other words, one person now holds about as much wealth as an entire wealthy nation produces in a year.
Some comparisons make the figure easier to grasp.
If you were handed one dollar every second,
it would take you thirty-four thousand nine hundred years to collect one point one trillion dollars —
a journey back to the age of the woolly mammoth.
And if all those dollar bills were laid end to end,
the line would wrap around the sun one hundred thirty-nine times.
Yet Musk's place as the first member of the trillionaire club, won through the SpaceX IPO,
is also a powerful symbol of the growing gap between rich and poor.
In January, the charity Oxfam reported that billionaire wealth had risen last year to its highest level ever recorded —
eighteen point three trillion dollars —
even though one in four people struggles to eat regularly and half the world's population lives in poverty.
The contrast becomes sharper with one example.
In 2021, during a public disagreement with Musk,
the World Food Programme laid out a detailed plan to spend six point six billion dollars and rescue forty-two million people who were close to starvation.
With one point one trillion dollars, that same plan could be funded for one hundred sixty-seven years.
